title: Mood differential and longitudinal course: how much do five days six years ago move?

objectives.statement: Rank the unipolar, bipolar-spectrum, medical, neurologic, medication, substance, grief, trauma, and contextual alternatives for a described mood presentation by the evidence that bears on each, and state for every alternative whether it sits low because the record counters it, because nobody asked, or because no history can settle it.

Judge a single item of past history on two separate properties, how far it would move the differential if it happened as described and how far the channel that delivered it can be relied on, and name the second channel that would firm it.

Name the question, test, or period of prospective observation that would separate two named alternatives, state which way each possible result would move them, and record what remains unavailable rather than reasoning past it.

scenes.title: Five days, six years ago
scenes.contentHtml:
Five days, six years ago

Two clinicians read the same notes and disagree. Neither of them disagrees about the four months.

R. is 34 and works rotating night shifts in a warehouse. Four months of low mood and loss of interest. Waking at four in the morning and not getting back to sleep. Still going to work, and slipping at it. No longer seeing friends. About 6 kg lost over the same period, without trying. Alcohol most evenings, more of it over the last two months, which R. says is to get to sleep. Cold, constipated, and tired past what the lost sleep would explain. No thyroid result in the file. A parent had "nerves" and took lithium for years; R. knows nothing further. Asked directly, R. describes stretches when life does not feel worth the effort, with no plan, no intent, and nothing done.

And six years ago, about five days of sleeping very little, being unusually busy and talkative, and buying several things on impulse. Nobody assessed it at the time. R. calls it a good patch.

The first clinician treats those five days as the most informative sentence in the file. The second treats them as one cheerful week in someone's late twenties, described once, six years later, by a person who is depressed now and has every reason to remember an energetic week warmly.

Neither of them doubts that R. is depressed. They differ over what kind of course this episode belongs to, and the episode in front of them cannot settle that on its own. At the moment of the interview a first depressive episode and the depressed phase of a bipolar-spectrum course, meaning a course in which episodes of elevated or activated mood have also occurred, present much alike. What separates them sits in the past, or has not happened yet.

Run the same problem forwards and it looks like this. In a United States population cohort of 6,214 adults with a lifetime diagnosis of major depressive disorder, 4.0% had a manic episode within about three years of follow-up. Some of the people who present as R. presents will look different later, and nothing available at a first appointment says which.

So the five days are load-bearing. The question is how much one sentence of remembered history can be asked to carry, and what it would take to find out.

What this lesson does

You will work R.'s file as a differential: a set of alternatives, each supported, weakened, or simply untested by particular items of evidence. By the end you should be able to:

  • rank unipolar, bipolar-spectrum, medical, neurologic, medication, substance, grief, trauma, and contextual alternatives by the evidence that bears on each, and say for every one whether it sits low because the record counters it or because nobody has looked;
  • judge a single item of past history on two separate properties, how far it would move the differential if it happened as described and how reliable the channel that delivered it is, and say what a second channel would add;
  • name the evidence, test, or period of observation that would separate two named alternatives, state which way each possible result would move them, and record what stays unavailable.

Two words first. Depression here always names the clinical syndrome and never the ordinary sense of feeling low. Passive thoughts is the term used later for what R. describes at the end of that summary: thoughts of not wanting to go on, carrying no plan, no intent, and no act.

Three things this lesson leans on and does not teach. Assembling the mood picture itself, with its time course and the source of each observation, belongs to mood phenomenology and function (PSY-250.01). Stating a working formulation with its confidence and inviting correction belongs to communicating and updating a formulation (PSY-210.06). The passive thoughts R. reports are recorded here as part of the picture and are worked as a safety question in collaborative crisis planning (PSY-230.06) and in safety and uncertainty in mood presentations (PSY-250.03). What comes after the differential, meaning anything anyone might do about it, belongs to the treatment outcomes (PSY-250.04 and PSY-250.05) and is out of scope here.

Check
id check-what-would-change-your-mind

Before reading on, write two lines and keep them.

  1. On what you have read so far, which two alternatives would you put at the top, and what in the file puts them there?
  2. Name one thing you could find out this week that would change that order. Say which way the result would move it.

You will compare both lines with your own later answers. The second is what the lesson is about.

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. R. is invented for reasoning practice and is not a real patient, a composite of real patients, or a claim about how often any of this occurs. This lesson does not reach a diagnosis for R., and nothing in it is a basis for assessing, diagnosing, or treating anyone.

Source Note
claims claim-cross-sectional-underdetermines-course, claim-mdd-to-bipolar-transition-ratesources source-gilman-nesarc, source-odonovan-alda

The transition figure comes from a prospective population study that reinterviewed adults with major depressive disorder about three years later; it describes that cohort over that interval and is not a prediction about any individual. A review of depression preceding bipolar diagnosis supports the wider point that the features separating the two courses are longitudinal. Everything about R. is written for this lesson.

scenes.title: Every item of history has two prices
scenes.contentHtml:
Every item of history has two prices

A differential that lists nine categories and stops is a textbook page. A differential that works is a ranked set of alternatives, each one carrying the evidence that put it where it is and the next thing that would move it.

Ranking needs a unit of reasoning smaller than the alternative. That unit is the item of evidence, and each item has two separate properties that are easy to collapse into one.

Definition
id definition-weightlabel Weight

Weight is how far an item would move the ranking if it happened exactly as described. It is read off the content of the item against the rest of the file, so a new item elsewhere can raise or lower it. What it never depends on is whether this particular item is true.

Definition
id definition-channellabel Channel

Channel is the route by which the item reached you, and how much that route can be relied on for this kind of content. It is a property of the evidence, and it does not depend on how interesting the content is.

An item with high weight and a weak channel is the ordinary case in a mood history, and it is the one people get wrong in both directions. Treating it as settled overreads it. Discarding it because the channel is weak throws away the most informative thing in the file. The move that works is to state both judgements separately, then name the second channel that would firm the item up.

The lithium in R.'s family

Take a line from the file that is not the five days.

A parent had "nerves" and took lithium for years; R. knows nothing further.

Weight, if true. Among the features of a depressive presentation that predict a later bipolar diagnosis, family history of bipolar disorder is the best replicated, alongside early onset, a recurrent course, and subthreshold hypomanic or mixed features, meaning features of an elevated or mixed state that fell short of an episode in duration or in number. A confirmed parental bipolar disorder would move the bipolar-spectrum alternative up substantially, and it is the strongest thing a family history can contribute.

What the file actually contains. A family history of long-term lithium use, reported second-hand, attached to a folk word for distress. Long-term lithium is a strong pointer without being a diagnosis: what the file holds is R.'s account of a treatment decision made for someone else, years ago, which R. did not witness and cannot describe. Getting from that to a confirmed parental bipolar disorder takes one inferential step, and the step is not free.

Channel. R.'s account of a parent's treatment, unverified, non-specific, and given while R. is depressed.

Second channel. Ask R. to ask. Or, with consent, seek the prescribing record. This is a cheap question with a large answer, and it is the kind of thing that gets left out of a first assessment because it is nobody's job in the room.

The item did not resolve. Its rank went from "strong bipolar pointer" to "one confirmable question away from a strong bipolar pointer", which is a different instruction to whoever sees R. next.

Three kinds of longitudinal evidence

Definition
id definition-longitudinal-evidencelabel Longitudinal evidence

Longitudinal evidence is evidence about the shape of a person's illness over time: episodes, their order, their duration, what happened between them, and what changed alongside them.

It arrives by three channels, and they are not interchangeable.

Channel What it is Its characteristic weakness
Retrospective self-report The person's account of past episodes, given now Recall bias, and the weakest episodes are the hardest to recall
Collateral and records An informant who was present, or a document written at the time Availability, consent, and the informant's own vantage point
Prospective observation What you and the person record from today forward It takes the time it takes

Only the third is a channel you can create, and it answers the question you set it. Write down in advance what you are watching for and what each possible outcome would mean, or three months later you will be reconstructing the period from memory and holding a second retrospective account with the weaknesses of the first.

Four states an alternative can be in

When you finish ranking, every alternative on the list is in one of four states, and the four are not degrees of the same thing.

  1. Supported. Something in the record speaks for it.
  2. Countered. Something in the record speaks against it.
  3. Unassessed. Nothing speaks either way, because the question was not asked.
  4. Not answerable from history. The evidence that would settle it is a test or an observation period, and no further conversation will produce it.

An alternative sitting low because it was never asked about is a finding about the assessment and says nothing about the person. Writing "no history of trauma" when nobody asked is the commonest way a differential launders an absence into a negative. States 3 and 4 are the part of the output that generates work, because each one names a specific thing to do next.

Check
id check-weight-channel-split

For each of these three lines from R.'s file, say in one sentence what its weight would be if true, and in one sentence what channel delivered it. Rank nothing yet; that comes two scenes from here.

  1. "About 6 kg lost over four months, without trying."
  2. "Alcohol most evenings, increased over the last two months, to help with sleep."
  3. "No thyroid function result available."

One of the three is not the same kind of thing as the other two.

The third line is not an item of history. It is the record telling you which state one of your alternatives is in: not answerable from history, and cheap to answer another way. That is worth writing down in exactly those words. The first two lines are worked in the two scenes that follow.

Source Note
claims claim-family-history-strongest-predictor, claim-retrospective-recall-biassources source-odonovan-alda, source-regeer

A review of depressive presentations that later turn out to be bipolar supports family history as the best-replicated predictor and lists the other features that travel with it. It also supports the point about recall, which the general-population reappraisal study puts numbers to in the next scene. Neither source says anything about R., about lithium in R.'s family, or about what any individual's family history means for that individual.

scenes.title: Working the five days
scenes.contentHtml:
Working the five days

Worked Example
id worked-example-five-days

Task. Decide how far the five days six years ago move the bipolar-spectrum alternative in R.'s differential, and name what would firm the answer. Do not decide what R. has.

What the file gives. About five days. Sleeping very little. Unusually busy. Unusually talkative. Several impulsive purchases. Six years ago. Never assessed by anyone. R.'s own word for it: a good patch.

What the file does not give. Whether the state was a change from R.'s usual self that other people could see. Whether R. needed less sleep that week or simply got less of it, which are different observations and the file records only the second. What else was going on that week, including R.'s shift pattern, any new medicine, and anything taken to stay awake. Whether the purchases had consequences R. is still carrying. Whether anything similar has happened since. Who else was around to notice.

Model selected. Weight and channel, judged separately, because this item scores high on one and low on the other and a single verdict would hide that.

Plan. State the weight. State the channel, with the specific bias that applies to this kind of content. Check whether any threshold argument is doing work here. Say what the next channel would be. Write the conclusion in a form the next clinician can act on.

Weight, if it happened as described. High, and higher than anything else in the file. A period of days with reduced sleep, increased activity, increased talkativeness and disinhibited spending, occurring as a departure from the person's usual state, is the observation that reclassifies the present picture. It changes which course R. is understood to be in, and therefore which questions matter at every later contact. No other single sentence available in one conversation does that.

Channel, and the bias that applies. A single retrospective self-report, six years old, given by a person who is currently depressed, about a state that people are known to under-recognise. In a Dutch general-population study, 40 adults who met research criteria for lifetime bipolar disorder were reinterviewed. Nine recognised having had hypomanic or manic episodes, and seven had ever consulted a professional about one. In the same 40 people, 33 recognised their depressive episodes and 30 had consulted someone about those. Roughly a fifth had noticed the elevated side against roughly four fifths for the depressed side. Among those who did not recognise the elevated episodes, the reasons given most often were that the periods had been pleasant and productive, or felt like part of the person's personality.

R. says: a good patch.

R.'s phrasing matches the commonest reason people give for not recognising an episode, and the inference that suggests itself here runs backwards. The match removes one reason to discount the report, namely the assumption that R. would have raised the week as a problem if it had been one. It supplies no positive evidence that the state was hypomanic. A pleasant, productive week is also what a pleasant, productive week feels like. The study found low self-recognition among people who have the condition; it says nothing about how often people who do not have it describe past weeks in those terms, and reading it that way converts a finding about one group into a claim about one person.

Is a threshold doing any work here? The convention in widest use sets a minimum of four days for hypomania. R.'s five clears it, so duration is not what limits this case, which is fortunate given what the convention rests on. That four-day minimum entered practice with DSM-IV in 1994. An international group publishing research criteria, its authors including those of the long-running Zurich cohort, states that no empirical evidence supports the particular cut-off and sets the minimum at two days instead, citing studies of shorter episodes; other commentators argue that moving the line down would widen bipolar diagnosis further, and the argument is unsettled. Had R. said three days, the label would have changed and the evidence would not have.

The next channel. Someone who knew R. six years ago and would remember that week. With R.'s consent, one conversation with that person would move this item further than any amount of additional questioning of R., because the limit here is the channel and not the description. The parent's prescribing history is the second such question and costs about as little.

Independent check. Try changing one thing at a time and see what moves.

Change What moves
Five days becomes three The label under the current convention. Not the evidence, and not what you would do next.
R. adds that a friend called it frightening The channel improves without the content changing, and the ranking moves more than any duration change could.
R. adds that the week ran across six night shifts A competing explanation for the reduced sleep appears, and the item's weight drops until that is unpicked.
R. adds two similar weeks in the last two years Recurrence enters the record, and the item stops being a single retrospective report.

Three of those four changes are questions you could ask this afternoon.

Interpretation. The bipolar-spectrum alternative is live, resting on one retrospective self-report of about five days of reduced sleep with increased activity, talkativeness and impulsive spending six years ago, never assessed, described by R. in positive terms. It is not established. Whether it is the leading alternative depends on the rest of the list, which is not yet worked. It is confirmable in principle, by an informant account of that week and by the parent's prescribing history, and both are available.

That is the output. Someone reading it next month can act on it without asking R. to tell the story again.

Self-explanation. Which did more to raise the bipolar-spectrum alternative: the content of R.'s five days, or the fact that R. described them warmly? Answer in one sentence, then say what would have to be true for the other answer to be right.

A defensible answer names the content. The warmth of the description is consistent with a hypomanic period going unrecognised and equally consistent with a good week being remembered as a good week, so on its own it moves nothing. It belongs in the note for a different reason: it explains why the episode was never assessed, which tells the next reader why this part of the history is thin instead of leaving them to guess.

Source Note
claims claim-hypomania-self-recognition-low, claim-hypomania-duration-threshold-contested, claim-retrospective-recall-biassources source-regeer, source-ghaemi-crdc, source-odonovan-alda

The recognition figures come from a reappraisal of 40 people from a Dutch general-population survey, so they describe that small sample and the study's diagnostic method; they are not a rate at which any individual's memory is wrong. The duration convention is reported here from a research-criteria paper by an international group who argue the four-day cut-off is arbitrary and propose two days; the same paper records that others expect a lower threshold to widen diagnosis, and this lesson takes no position on where the line should sit. The point about recall bias in past-episode reports comes from a review of depressive presentations that later prove bipolar.

scenes.title: The drink and the four o'clock waking
scenes.contentHtml:
The drink and the four o'clock waking

Check
id check-predict-alcohol-role

Commit to an answer before reading on. R. drinks most evenings, has drunk more over the last two months, and says it is to get to sleep. R. has been waking at four for four months.

Write one sentence saying what you think the alcohol is doing to the sleep, and one sentence saying what would show you were wrong.

Misconception
id misconception-alcohol-explains-the-sleep

The model to examine. R. drinks in the evening. Alcohol breaks up the second half of the night. The four o'clock waking is the drink, so it should be taken out of the depressive picture rather than counted in it.

Why it is worth taking seriously. The mechanism is real and it fits the clock. Evening alcohol shortens the time to fall asleep and sedates through the first part of the night; arousal then rebounds two to three hours after blood alcohol falls close to zero, with rebound REM sleep and more awakenings through the second half. Someone drinking in the evening and waking around three or four in the morning is describing that curve. The hypnotic effect also fades within days of regular use, so the amount needed to get to sleep climbs, which is the loop R. is describing when R. says the drinking has increased and is for sleep.

The observation the model cannot absorb. The dates do not line up. The low mood and the four o'clock waking have been there four months. The increase in drinking covers the last two. An increase that began two months after the waking cannot have started the waking. R.'s own account puts the sleep problem first: the drinking is described as a response to it.

A model that holds both. Two mechanisms, running in the same direction, starting at different times. Something at four months opened the sleep problem. Alcohol at the current level is a strong candidate for holding it open now, and for having made it worse over the last two months. Those are separate claims, they carry different evidence, and only the second is well supported by the timeline in the file.

The same test applied to the whole picture. The question behind the misconception is larger than the sleep: is the depressive picture itself alcohol-related? The discriminator is chronology. Features that appear only during periods of problem drinking and clear during extended sobriety point one way; features that predate the drinking or persist through sobriety point the other. Two to four weeks of abstinence is usually advised before the picture is judged, because most symptoms and signs resolve within the first four weeks.

Applying that to R. gives a partial answer and exposes a gap. The four-month picture leads the two-month escalation, which argues against the whole presentation being a consequence of the recent drinking. But "most evenings" was true before the escalation as well, and the file does not record when that pattern started. Nobody asked. Until that date exists, the chronology argument runs on half its evidence.

One more thing the model gets wrong, in the other direction. If R. stopped drinking and the sleep did not improve, that would be tempting to read as proof that the sleep belongs to the depressive picture. It is weaker evidence than it looks. For close to half of people with alcohol dependence, sleep disturbance persists for months after the last drink. An observation period across abstinence is informative about mood and much less informative about sleep, and a plan that treats the two as one measurement will misread whatever it finds.

Recheck, three short cases. For each, say whether chronology favours an independent depressive picture, an alcohol-related one, or neither, and name the one further fact you would want.

  1. Low mood began three weeks after the drinking escalated, and lifted over three weeks of abstinence during an admission for something else.
  2. Low mood has been present in every one of four episodes over twelve years, two of which fell in periods with no drinking at all.
  3. Mood lifted over four weeks of abstinence; the four o'clock waking did not change.

The third is the one that separates readers. Abstinence is one intervention and the two symptoms answer to it on different timescales, so the mood response and the sleep response are two results, not one.

Source Note
claims claim-alcohol-rebound-second-half, claim-substance-chronology-discriminatorsources source-stein-friedmann, source-shivani

A review of disturbed sleep in alcohol use supports the shape of the night under evening alcohol, the loss of the sedating effect with regular use, and the persistence of sleep disturbance into abstinence for a large minority. A diagnostic review published by the United States National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism supports chronology as the discriminator between independent and alcohol-related psychiatric presentations and the two-to-four-week observation period. Neither source describes R., and neither supplies a rule for how any individual should manage their drinking; that question belongs to a clinician and the person concerned.

scenes.title: The rest of the list, in the state it is actually in
scenes.contentHtml:
The rest of the list, in the state it is actually in

Six alternatives are still unworked. Take them in order of how much support they have, with less help each time. For every one: what in the record speaks to it, what would move it and which way, and which of the four states it is in.

Completion problem: the thyroid

Most of this one is done for you. Finish the last column.

R. feels cold, is constipated, and is tired past what the lost sleep would explain. Those three sit among the usual presenting features of hypothyroidism, alongside lethargy, dry skin and weight gain. Against them: R. has lost about 6 kg without trying, and weight gain is the direction hypothyroidism usually pushes. Against them again, more quietly: a four-month depressive picture with reduced intake and reduced activity explains the constipation and the weight loss without needing a thyroid at all. Individual symptoms are poor at identifying hypothyroidism, they overlap other conditions, and the diagnosis is made by measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine.

Question Answer
What speaks for it Cold intolerance, constipation, fatigue disproportionate to the sleep loss
What speaks against it Unintentional weight loss; a competing explanation for two of the three features
Which state ?
What would move it, and which way ?

The state is not answerable from history. No further conversation will settle it, and one blood test will. That is the whole reason the missing result is worth writing in the note as a missing result instead of reasoning past it.

The second answer needs more care than it usually gets. A normal result removes an alternative and does nothing else. A mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine is a common finding when depressed people are tested, and large observational studies together with small intervention studies have not established that it causes or worsens depression; correcting it often leaves the depressive symptoms where they were. So a mildly abnormal result does not hand you an explanation. It hands you a second finding that then has to be argued for.

Two arguments about thyroid testing get run together and they are different arguments. One is about testing everyone with a depressive presentation, where the usual result is the mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone described above and the causal reading of it has not held up. The other is about testing a person who has cold intolerance, constipation, and disproportionate fatigue, which is a symptom-driven question. R. is in the second, and the evidence about the first does not settle it.

Supported problem: the shifts

R. works rotating night shifts. Work through this one with two prompts.

Prompt one. Night-shift workers were about 40% more likely to develop depression than day workers in a meta-analysis of eleven studies, individual studies of major depressive disorder specifically have gone both ways, and whether circadian disruption causes mood disorder, follows from it, or accompanies it without causing either is unresolved. Given that, what does the shift work earn on the list?

Prompt two. The file says R. wakes at four in the morning and does not get back to sleep. In a rotating-shift worker, what would you need to know before that sentence means anything?

A contextual alternative competes at the level of explanation, not at the level of label, so the useful question is how much of the picture it accounts for and whether changing it would change the course. Here it earns a place as a plausible contributor with an unresolved direction of causation, which is a weaker claim than the association alone might suggest.

The second prompt is the one that pays. Four o'clock means one thing in a person who sleeps from eleven to seven and something else in a person whose sleep window moved twice last week. Until you know R.'s shift pattern across the four months, one of the most-quoted features of the presentation is uninterpretable. That is a free question and nobody has asked it.

Independent problems: the neurological and the medication alternatives

No prompts. Work both, then read on.

Neurological alternatives, in a 34-year-old with no reported focal signs, no reported cognitive change, and no reported neurological history, sit low on what is in the file. Before recording them as countered, check whether the assessment covered them. If the notes are silent because the questions were not asked, the state is unassessed, and the two states get written differently. An absence that has been looked for and an absence that has not been looked for are worth different amounts, and the note is the only place that difference survives.

The medication alternative is starker. The file contains no medication list. More than a dozen classes of general medical drug have been associated with depressive symptoms, an association between taking a drug and becoming depressed is not by itself a causal relation, and the arguments that carry weight are temporal: onset after starting or increasing a drug, and resolution after reducing or stopping it. None of that reasoning can begin without a list. The alternative is not low. It has not been entered.

Independent problems: grief and trauma

Nothing in R.'s file speaks to either, in either direction, because neither was asked about.

Prolonged grief is descriptively distinct from depression and from post-traumatic stress, with separation distress and yearning for the person who died as its distinguishing features, and the three co-occur often enough that finding one is no reason to stop looking for the others. Longitudinal work in bereaved adults finds their symptoms tracking one another across measurement waves, with the direction of influence unsettled. Trauma exposure is found the same way, by asking.

Both are unassessed. Writing "no history of loss or trauma" when the question was not put is the commonest way a differential turns an absence of asking into a negative finding, and it is the one entry on this list that a later reader has no way to detect.

Mixed selection

Now rank the whole list for R. on current evidence, with a state for each. Do this from memory before comparing.

Alternative State on current evidence
Unipolar depressive course Supported. The four-month picture is the evidence, and it remains the alternative the record best fits.
Bipolar-spectrum course Live and second, on one retrospective self-report and one confirmable family-history lead. Not established.
Substance-related Contributing, and unlikely to be the whole picture on the two-month lead. Missing: when the evening drinking started.
Medical, thyroid Not answerable from history. One test outstanding.
Contextual, shift work and circadian disruption Plausible contributor, direction unresolved, and it makes one recorded feature uninterpretable until the shift pattern is known.
Neurologic Low on what is recorded; check whether it was asked before calling it countered.
Medication Not entered. No medication list exists.
Grief Unassessed.
Trauma Unassessed.

Unipolar sitting top is not a conclusion about R. It is a description of a ranking that still contains unasked questions, an absent medication list, and an unrequested blood test. Any of those could move it, and most of them could be closed before the end of the day.

Source Note
claims claim-hypothyroid-symptoms-nonspecific, claim-subclinical-hypothyroid-depression-link-unestablishedsources source-zamwar, source-samuels

A review of hypothyroidism supports the usual presenting features, their non-specificity, the usual direction of weight change, and the tests that establish the diagnosis. A commentary in a clinical endocrinology journal supports the point that mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine is common in tested depressed patients and that a causal link to depression has not been established. Neither source recommends or discourages testing any individual, and this lesson makes no recommendation about anyone's investigations.

Source Note
claims claim-shift-work-depression-association, claim-medication-attribution-hard, claim-grief-distinct-overlappingsources source-walker, source-rogers-pies, source-janshen-eisma

The shift-work figure is quoted by a review of circadian disruption and mental health from a meta-analysis of eleven studies; the same review records that studies of major depressive disorder specifically have been mixed and that the direction of causation is unresolved. A review of general medical drugs associated with depression supports the breadth of the drug classes involved and the difficulty of attributing cause. A systematic review of eight longitudinal studies in 2,914 bereaved adults supports prolonged grief being descriptively distinct from depression and post-traumatic stress while frequently co-occurring with them. None of these sources describes shift patterns, medicines, or losses in R.'s life, because those are not in the file.

scenes.title: Transfer: a file where the good channel is the one nobody used
scenes.contentHtml:
Transfer: a file where the good channel is the one nobody used

Different person, different shape. The method is the one you have.

T. is 61. T.'s partner died suddenly fourteen months ago. T. had a heart attack ten months ago. A beta blocker was started eight months ago and has continued since. T.'s daughter, who has come to the appointment, dates the change in her father to about nine months ago: low mood, loss of interest, waking early, and a flat quality she says is different from the first months after the death. T. does not drink. Neither T. nor his daughter recalls anything like this before. T.'s own summary is that he is old and sad now.

Four dates, in the order they happened: the death at fourteen months, the heart attack at ten, the mood change at nine, the beta blocker at eight.

Check
id check-transfer-tasks

Work these four before reading the discussion. Written answers, five minutes.

  1. Build the timeline and say which candidate the chronology supports and which it undercuts.
  2. The daughter is in the room. Name two questions you would put to her that you cannot put to T., and say why each one has to go to her.
  3. Give a state to each of: grief-related, depressive, medication, medical, bipolar-spectrum.
  4. Name the single item that would move the ranking most, and say which way each possible answer would move it.

One. The chronology cuts against the beta blocker as the thing that started this. The mood change is dated a month before the drug began. That is the same tool used on R.'s drinking, pointing the other way: there, an increase two months after the waking could not have started the waking; here, a drug started a month after the mood change could not have started the mood change. Neither result clears the substance. Beta blockers sit among the general medical drug classes associated with depressive symptoms, association is not causation in either direction, and the arguments that carry weight are temporal ones about starting, increasing, reducing and stopping. What the timeline does is retire one specific version of the medication claim and leave the weaker version standing. The heart attack, sitting a month before the mood change, is a temporal association of exactly the shape people find persuasive, and by itself it establishes nothing except that something else was happening then which nobody has yet listed.

Two. The daughter is the best channel in this file, and she is the only route to two questions T. cannot answer about himself. Whether the current state is a change from T.'s usual self, which is a comparison T. is poorly placed to make from inside it. And whether there has ever been a period of elevated, driven, or unusually active mood that T. would not think worth mentioning. In R.'s file that second question had no informant available and the assessment was limited by it. Here an informant is sitting in the room, and asking T. alone would reproduce R.'s limitation by choice.

Three. Grief-related is supported, with a real and dated loss. Depressive is supported, on the daughter's account of a change in quality after the early months. Those two are not competitors in the sense that only one may be true: prolonged grief is descriptively distinct from depression and from post-traumatic stress and the three co-occur often, so finding a death in the history is a reason to assess all three and not a reason to stop. Medication is entered, chronology against it as an initiator, open as a contributor. Medical is entered and thin: a heart attack at ten months means a hospital episode, a medication list, and a set of investigations that nobody in this room has looked at. Bipolar-spectrum is unassessed through the only channel that would answer it.

Four. Two answers are defensible and it is worth knowing why.

An account from the daughter of any past period of elevated or activated mood is the item that would change the category, not the weighting, and it costs one question. The full medication and investigation record from the cardiac admission is the item that would populate three alternatives at once, and it costs one request. Choose the first if you want the largest single move; choose the second if you want the largest reduction in how much of the file is unassessed. What is not defensible is leaving the appointment having asked T. about his mood and nobody about anything else.

The trap in this case. A death, then low mood, then a man who says he is old and sad. The pull is to write "bereavement" and stop, which turns a supported alternative into a conclusion and leaves four other alternatives unassessed on the grounds that one of them is plausible. The presence of a good explanation is not evidence against the others.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: what goes in the record, and what gets asked for
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: what goes in the record, and what gets asked for

Callout
id callout-wrap-up-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. R. and T. are invented. The note below is a model of how differential reasoning is written down, produced by this lesson's method on this lesson's fictional file. It is not a template for any real person's care, it reaches no diagnosis, and it is not a basis for requesting or interpreting anyone's investigations.

The appointment is ending. The clinical question is the one that always arrives at this point and rarely gets taught: what goes in the record, and what gets asked for before the next contact.

The note

Working differential, R., first assessment. Four months of low mood, loss of interest, waking at four and not returning to sleep, about 6 kg of unintentional weight loss, withdrawal from friends, and slipping performance at work, in a rotating night-shift worker who drinks most evenings and has drunk more over the last two months.

A unipolar depressive course fits the present picture and is the leading reading on current evidence.

A bipolar-spectrum course is the main alternative, live and not established. It rests on one item: R.'s account of about five days six years ago of markedly reduced sleep with increased activity, increased talkativeness and several impulsive purchases, never assessed at the time, described by R. as a good patch. The reported duration clears the usual four-day convention, so what is uncertain here is the report and not the threshold. A second and weaker item points the same way: a parent treated with lithium for years, details unknown to R. Both are confirmable with consent, by an informant who knew R. six years ago and by the parent's prescribing record.

Alcohol is contributing and is unlikely to account for the whole picture, because the mood change and the early waking lead the escalation in drinking by about two months. The current pattern is a strong candidate for holding the early waking open. The start date of the pre-escalation drinking is not recorded.

Thyroid disease is not answerable from the history and is untested. Cold intolerance, constipation and fatigue beyond the sleep loss point towards it; the unintentional weight loss points away.

Shift work and circadian disruption are plausible contributors of unresolved direction. The shift pattern across the four months is not recorded, and until it is, "wakes at four" cannot be read.

Not entered: medication, because no list was taken. Unassessed and not recorded either way: loss, trauma, and neurological enquiry.

Risk: passive thoughts that life is not worth the effort, no plan, no intent, no act, raised only on direct questioning. Carried to the safety formulation.

Five questions and one test

What What it buys What it does not buy
An informant account of the week six years ago The largest single move available, because it changes the channel on the highest-weight item A diagnosis. A friend's memory six years on is a better channel, not a certain one
The parent's prescribing history Turns "took lithium" into a family history or removes it Anything about R.'s own course
The shift pattern across the four months Makes the early-waking item readable and separates roster-driven sleep loss from the rest An explanation for the mood
When the evening drinking started Completes the chronology argument that currently runs on half its evidence The direction of causation
A medication list Lets the medication alternative be entered at all A cause, since association is not causation and only timing arguments carry weight
Thyroid function A normal result removes an alternative An explanation, if mildly abnormal. A raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine is common in tested depressed people and has not been shown to cause or worsen depression, so that result starts an argument instead of ending one

Five of the six are questions. One is a blood test. Nothing on the list is expensive, and the file has been carrying all six as silence.

The prospective part, written in advance

Waiting and watching is a channel you can create, and it counts as evidence only if the question is written before the watching starts. For R. that means recording three things, separately, against dates: mood, sleep, and the shift roster; any period of reduced sleep with increased activity, dated when it happens rather than recalled later; and, if drinking changes, the mood response and the sleep response noted as two results, because they run on different timescales and a plan that treats them as one measurement will misread whatever it finds.

Written that way, the next three months produce evidence. Written as "review in three months", they produce another retrospective account with the same weaknesses as the first one.

What this note refuses to do

It does not choose. Refusing to choose is not the same as being vague, and the difference is visible on the page: every alternative in that note carries a state, the evidence that put it there, and a named next step. "It could be many things" carries none of those, and it leaves the next clinician doing the whole assessment again.

The two readers from the first scene can both sign that note. They would still bet differently about R., and the note does not ask them not to. It fixes what they are betting on and what would settle it, which is the most a first conversation can produce.

The note also does not say what should be done about any of it. That question is real and it is the next one, and it belongs to the medication and interventional evidence outcome (PSY-250.04) and the psychological and social evidence outcome (PSY-250.05). Deciding between alternatives and deciding what to do are different pieces of reasoning, and the second one gets worse when the first is skipped.

Check
id check-compare-with-your-first-answer

Find the two lines you wrote at the start.

  1. Did your top two alternatives survive? If they changed, name the item of evidence that moved them.
  2. Your second line named one thing you could find out this week. Compare it with the six above. If yours is on the list, say which state it changes. If it is not, say what it would buy and whether you would still ask for it.

Then, without looking back, write the four states an alternative can be in and give an example of each from R.'s file.

Accessibility and alternatives

Every task here can be answered in prose, in bullets, or as a table, whichever suits you, and you may type, dictate, or work with a tutor. The tables repeat their logic in the surrounding prose and are read in normal reading order. Nothing depends on colour, position on a page, dragging, sound, motion, or a timed reveal. No task asks for your own health information, medication, diagnosis, or family history, and none requires contact with a patient, a clinic, or a laboratory.

This lesson describes low mood, alcohol use, bereavement, and passive thoughts about life not being worth the effort. If the material meets something in your own life, stop or step away without penalty. EmbeddedKnowledge does not monitor learners and provides no clinical or crisis service; for personal support use an appropriately qualified local service or your current emergency route.

Recovery route

The assessment is untimed and retakeable, and a missed criterion routes you to a specific reread instead of a repeat of the same case.

  • If the ranking came out as a list of labels with no evidence attached, redo the five days with weight and channel separated, then write the two sentences again before ranking anything.
  • If you gave every alternative the same state, reread the four states. Supported, countered, unassessed, and not answerable from history are different findings and they generate different next steps.
  • If "unassessed" and "countered" still blur, use the test that catches it: could a reader of this note tell whether the question was asked? If not, the entry is unassessed and should say so.
  • If the alcohol reasoning came out as either "it is the drink" or "it is not the drink", go back to the dates. Two mechanisms starting at different times is the answer the timeline supports, and the note has to carry both.
  • If you concluded that R. has a bipolar-spectrum disorder, or that R. does not, reread the worked example. The evidence supports neither conclusion, and reaching one is the specific failure this lesson is built to prevent.
  • If you are unsure how much confidence to state, that is the skill taught by communicating and updating a formulation (PSY-210.06), which this lesson assumes. Return here after it.

Where this goes next

Safety and uncertainty in mood presentations (PSY-250.03) is where the risk line in R.'s note gets worked properly. Longitudinal mood formulation (PSY-250.06) is where a differential like this one is revised against what the following months actually showed, which is the only way to find out whether the reasoning here was any good.

The note applies three sourced points: that the alternatives separating a unipolar from a bipolar-spectrum course are longitudinal rather than cross-sectional; that chronology is the discriminator between an independent and an alcohol-related presentation; and that a mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine in a depressed person has not been shown to cause or worsen the depression. assessment.title: Mood differential and longitudinal course mastery check

items.prompt: An invented file. K. is 41, a delivery driver, and describes seven months of low mood, loss of interest, waking two hours early, and eating less. K. takes a beta blocker started three years ago for migraine and prednisolone started five weeks ago for a chest problem. K. drinks at weekends only, unchanged for years. K. attends alone. Asked about earlier periods, K. says there was a spell in the twenties when everything was easy and money went quickly, but K. cannot date it and is not sure it lasted more than a couple of days. K.'s brother is described as 'up and down' with no further detail. No physical symptoms are recorded and no examination or blood test has been done. Rank the unipolar, bipolar-spectrum, medical, neurologic, medication, substance, grief, trauma, and contextual alternatives for K. For every one, give its state as supported, countered, unassessed, or not answerable from history, and give the evidence or the absence that puts it there.

answer.correct: Unipolar depressive course: supported, on the seven-month picture. Bipolar-spectrum: live on two weak items, an undated and possibly very brief period of ease and free spending reported by K. alone, and a brother described as up and down with no detail; both are single-channel and both are confirmable, so the state is supported but not established, and the undated brevity means no duration convention can be applied to it at all. Medication: supported and the strongest medical-side item, because prednisolone was started five weeks ago and the mood picture is seven months old, so the steroid cannot have started it but the timing of any change five weeks ago should be asked about; the beta blocker at three years is temporally uninformative for a seven-month change. Medical: not answerable from history, since no examination and no blood test have been done; the file records no physical symptoms, which is weaker than a normal result. Substance: countered as an initiator, because weekend-only drinking is unchanged for years, and it remains worth dating. Contextual: unassessed, since nothing about K.'s work pattern, sleep opportunity, or circumstances is recorded. Neurologic: unassessed rather than countered, because no neurological history, examination or cognitive enquiry appears. Grief: unassessed. Trauma: unassessed.
answer.summary: One supported alternative, one live but unestablished, one supported medication item whose chronology is partly against it, one substance item countered as an initiator, one not answerable from history, and four unassessed.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for placing unipolar and bipolar-spectrum with their evidence, including the observation that K.'s remembered spell is undated and possibly brief so no duration convention can be applied to it. Award one point for the medication reasoning: prednisolone is recent and cannot have started a seven-month picture while remaining worth asking about, and a drug started three years ago carries no temporal argument for a seven-month change. Award one point for correctly separating countered from unassessed, which requires substance to be countered as an initiator on the unchanged pattern, and neurologic, grief, trauma and contextual to be unassessed rather than low. Award one point for recording the medical alternative as not answerable from history and for stating that an absence of recorded physical symptoms is not a negative examination. A response that writes 'no history of trauma' or 'no medical cause' as findings loses the third and fourth points, because that is the specific error the lesson repairs. On a retry, rank a different invented file: a 27-year-old with five months of low mood, an aunt with a mood disorder of unspecified type, isotretinoin started six months ago, a partner attending who describes a fortnight last year of very little sleep and constant plans, and no bloods taken.
acceptableResponses: Any response that assigns all nine alternatives a state from the four, attaches the evidence or the absence that justifies each, distinguishes countered from unassessed, and treats the undated brief spell as evidence too weak to carry a duration argument.
commonErrors: Recording unassessed alternatives as negative findings
Treating prednisolone as the explanation because steroids are associated with mood change, without checking that the mood picture predates it by months
Applying a duration threshold to an episode K. cannot date
Calling the medical alternative countered because no physical symptoms are recorded
Ranking by how common each condition is rather than by the evidence in the file

items.prompt: Take one line from K.'s file: 'a spell in the twenties when everything was easy and money went quickly; K. cannot date it and is not sure it lasted more than a couple of days.' Write three short paragraphs. First, its weight if it happened as described. Second, its channel, naming the specific bias that applies to this kind of content and what is known about how strong that bias is. Third, the second channel you would seek and what it would and would not settle. Then answer in one sentence: does the reported brevity of the spell make it less informative, and why?

answer.correct: Weight: high if true, because a period of elevated or activated mood that was a change from K.'s usual state would move the presentation from a depressive episode to a depressive episode in a bipolar-spectrum course, which changes the expected course and the questions asked at every later contact. Channel: weak. A single undated retrospective self-report, given while depressed, about a kind of state that people under-recognise; in one general-population reappraisal only about a fifth of people with a research diagnosis of bipolar disorder recognised having had hypomanic or manic episodes, and the commonest explanations offered were that the periods had been pleasant and productive or felt like part of the person's personality. Milder and briefer episodes are the hardest to recall, and this one is reported as both. Second channel: an informant who knew K. in that period, with K.'s consent, asked whether the state was a visible change from K.'s usual self and how long it ran. That would improve the reliability of the report and would still not establish a diagnosis. Brevity: reported brevity lowers what the item can support under the duration convention in widest use, and it is a weaker argument than it looks, because that four-day minimum entered practice with DSM-IV in 1994, a research-criteria group states no empirical evidence supports the particular cut-off and proposes two days, and others hold that lowering it would widen bipolar diagnosis; here the deeper problem is that K. cannot date the spell at all, so no threshold can be applied to it either way.
answer.summary: High weight, weak channel with a named and quantified under-recognition bias, an informant as the second channel, and a brevity argument that turns out to be blocked by the absence of a date.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for a weight statement that says what the item would reclassify rather than merely calling it important. Award one point for a channel statement that names retrospective under-recognition of elevated states and gives the study's scale and limits, including that the finding describes people who have the condition and cannot be read backwards as a diagnostic sign. Award one point for a second channel that is a person and a specific question, together with an honest statement that it improves reliability without establishing a diagnosis. Award one point for the last sentence only if it both reports that the duration convention is contested and notices that an undated spell cannot be tested against any threshold. A response that treats the four-day convention as settled, in either direction, does not earn the fourth point. On a retry, do the same for a line reading: 'partner reports a fortnight last year of very little sleep and constant plans, which the partner found alarming.' Notice that the channel is now the strong one and the weight statement barely changes.
acceptableResponses: Any response that separates weight from channel, quantifies or bounds the under-recognition bias from the lesson's evidence, proposes a specific informant question as the second channel, and identifies the missing date as the reason no duration argument can run.
commonErrors: Collapsing weight and channel into a single verdict on the item
Reading low self-recognition backwards, so that a warmly described past week becomes evidence of hypomania
Applying the four-day convention as though it were settled
Proposing 'further history from the patient' as the second channel, which is the same channel again
Claiming an informant account would confirm the diagnosis

items.prompt: Still on K.'s file. Write the four requests you would make before the next contact. For each, state which two alternatives it separates, what each possible result would mean, and one thing it would not settle. Then write the two-sentence entry you would leave in the record about what is missing, in a form that tells the next reader which questions were asked and which were not.

answer.correct: A defensible set: an informant account of the spell in K.'s twenties and of any similar period, which separates unipolar from bipolar-spectrum, where a description of a visible change from usual self raises the second and no recollection leaves the first where it is; it would not date the spell reliably. Detail of the brother's 'up and down', which separates the same two, where a confirmed bipolar diagnosis in a first-degree relative raises the bipolar-spectrum alternative and a different or absent diagnosis removes a weak pointer; it says nothing about K.'s own course. Physical examination and basic bloods including thyroid function, which separates medical from psychiatric alternatives, where a normal result removes an alternative and a raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine starts an argument instead of ending one, because that pattern is common in tested depressed people and has not been shown to cause or worsen depression; it would not explain the seven months. A dated medication history covering the prednisolone start and any dose changes, which separates a medication-related from an independent picture, where a step change in mood at the start or at a dose change supports the drug and a mood picture unchanged across both leaves it aside; association alone would still not establish cause. Asking about losses, trauma, work pattern and sleep opportunity is a fifth legitimate answer and may replace any of the above if it is argued. The record entry must say which questions were put and which were not, for example: 'Loss, trauma, neurological history and work pattern were not covered at this contact and are not recorded either way. No examination or blood test has been done; the absence of recorded physical symptoms is an absence of enquiry, not a negative finding.'
answer.summary: Four requests, each tied to the pair of alternatives it separates, with the meaning of each possible result and an explicit limit, plus a record entry that distinguishes questions not asked from findings that were negative.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for requests that are each attached to a named pair of alternatives rather than listed as general workup. Award one point for stating what each possible result would mean in both directions, including the thyroid result whose mildly abnormal form does not supply an explanation. Award one point for a stated limit on each request, since a request presented as decisive is the error this item tests. Award one point for a record entry that a later reader could use to tell an unasked question from a negative finding. Any response whose record entry could be read as 'no history of trauma' does not earn the fourth point. On a retry, write the requests for the invented 27-year-old described in the first item's retry, where the partner is present and the drug is recent.
acceptableResponses: Any four defensible requests, each naming the pair of alternatives it separates, the meaning of each possible result, and a stated limit, with a record entry that separates unasked questions from negative findings.
commonErrors: Listing investigations as a routine panel with no alternative attached
Treating a mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone as an explanation for the depressive picture
Writing a record entry that reads as a negative finding for a question nobody asked
Naming only what would confirm an alternative and not what would lower it
Recommending a treatment change as the discriminating step

items.prompt: In an invented file, M. has had low mood and early waking for six months and has drunk heavily every evening for the last six weeks, saying it is to get to sleep. After four weeks of observed abstinence during an unrelated hospital admission, M.'s mood has clearly improved and the early waking is unchanged. Which reading does the evidence best support?

options.text: The unchanged early waking shows the depressive picture is independent of the drinking, because a symptom that survives abstinence cannot be alcohol-related.

The mood response is informative and the unchanged sleep is much less so, because sleep disturbance commonly persists for months into abstinence, so the two symptoms answer to abstinence on different timescales and give two results rather than one.
The improvement over four weeks shows the whole presentation was alcohol-related, since most symptoms resolve within the first four weeks of abstinence.
Nothing can be concluded, because six weeks of heavy drinking is too short a period for any chronology argument to apply.

answer.summary: Abstinence produces two results on two timescales; the mood response carries information and the unchanged sleep carries much less.
answer.reasoning: Abstinence is one intervention and the two symptoms respond to it differently. Most symptoms resolve within the first four weeks of abstinence, which is why the two-to-four-week observation period is advised, so a clear mood improvement across four weeks is a real result. Sleep is the documented exception: for close to half of people with alcohol dependence it stays disturbed for months after the last drink, so unchanged early waking is weak evidence in either direction. The first option treats an exception as a rule. The third overreads the mood improvement and ignores the six-month lead of the mood picture over the six-week escalation, which argues against the drinking having started it. The fourth abandons a chronology argument that has usable dates on both sides. If you chose the first or third, write both symptom timelines out separately against the abstinence date before answering. On a retry, decide the same question for a file where the mood is unchanged after four weeks and the early waking has settled.
commonErrors: Treating any symptom that survives abstinence as proof of an independent disorder
Reading improvement across an abstinence period as proof that alcohol caused everything
Merging the mood result and the sleep result into a single verdict
Discarding a chronology argument that has dates available on both sides

rubrics.title: Ranking a differential by the evidence in the file

criteria.description: Places the unipolar and bipolar-spectrum alternatives with the evidence that puts them there, and notes that an undated, possibly very brief remembered spell cannot carry a duration argument.
Reasons about the two drugs by chronology: a five-week-old steroid cannot have started a seven-month picture yet is worth asking about, and a three-year-old drug carries no temporal argument for it.
Separates countered from unassessed correctly across substance, neurologic, grief, trauma, and contextual alternatives.
Records the medical alternative as not answerable from history and states that no recorded physical symptoms is an absence of enquiry rather than a negative examination.

rubrics.title: Judging one item of longitudinal history

criteria.description: States what the item would reclassify if true, rather than asserting that it is important.
Names the under-recognition of past elevated states as the channel bias, bounds it with the lesson's evidence, and does not read that evidence backwards as a diagnostic sign.
Proposes a specific person and a specific question as the second channel, and states that it improves reliability without establishing a diagnosis.
Reports the duration convention as contested and identifies the missing date as the reason no threshold argument can run on this item at all.

rubrics.title: Naming what would separate two alternatives

criteria.description: Each request names the pair of alternatives it separates instead of being listed as general workup.
States what each possible result would mean in both directions, including a mildly abnormal thyroid result that does not supply an explanation.
Gives each request an explicit limit, so that none is presented as decisive.
Writes a record entry from which a later reader can tell an unasked question from a negative finding.

rubrics.title: Reading an abstinence period as two results

criteria.description: Selects the reading in which the mood response and the sleep response are two results on different timescales.
Rejects both the reading that a surviving symptom proves independence and the reading that improvement proves the drinking caused everything.
